newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Millionth copy for Angela's Ashes, epic of Irish woe.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Millionth copy for Angela's Ashes, epic of Irish woe.

text.p: When Frank McCourt sat down to write his memoir about growing up hungry and poor in an Irish slum during the 1930s he barely even expected a review.
Instead McCourt was inundated with praise, won a Pulitzer Prize and the first week of June he'll sell the millionth copy of "Angela's Ashes."

Since its release last September, the touching memoir has been translated into a dozen languages and has sold at a rate of nearly 100,000 copies a month in North America alone, where it has remained at the top of bestseller lists and is in its 36th printing.
"I thought it might get a respectful review in the New York Times, nothing like what's happened," the 66-year-old former New York school teacher said in a recent interview.

The wry, white-haired Irishman is about to join only a handful of authors in an exclusive club in the ever-competitive publishing industry where book dealers are delighted if a first printing sells out.

Last year only nine hardcover books published in 1996 reached the one million mark, all by well-known authors such as John Grisham ("The Runaway Jury) Tom Clancy ("Executive Orders") and Oprah Winfrey and Bob Greene ("Make the Connection"), according to the trade magazine Publisher's Weekly.
"It's extremely unusual for a new author to see his first book reach one million copies sold. It went beyond the expectations of the publishing community," said Jeff Zaleski, an editor at the Weekly.

McCourt's publisher, Scribner, agrees. "We've always had expectations, but I don't think we ever dared to foresee a million copies. Even the most ambitious publishers don't think quite that big," said Scribner publisher Susan Moldow.
"This book has defied all odds," she said, adding that the rights to the book have been sold to 13 countries.
Moldow said she expects the millionth copy to be rung up around June 1.

To celebrate the event Scribner plans a party to honour McCourt and his epic of woe, which recounts a childhood coping with a drunken father and a mother resigned to a poverty that cost her the lives of three children.
McCourt has said it took nearly thirty years to recover the voice of his childhood, which had been hidden beneath layers of anger and bitterness.
"Most people don't like to brag: 'Look at me, I grew up in a slum!'" he said at a recent public reading in Brooklyn, where he had lived and taught for many years.
"But I had always encouraged my students to tell me about their lives and write about it. And finally I realised I had to follow my own advice."
His lyrical but streetwise prose worked, finding an audience among rich and poor, and a movie deal with "Jaws" producer David Brown.
But the big question now is whether McCourt can touch as many lives again in his planned sequel, which will pick up where "Angela's Ashes" left off -- McCourt in the New World at age 19.
"I'm not a linear person who can write a book from start to finish with a story outline in advance," said the author, who has set a February 1998 deadline for the sequel.
"I'll go back into the mind of that bewildered 19-year-old I was," McCourt added. "I was really dense. It will be an epic of density."
